orders.rationale: The two answers are nearly identical and both correct: espresso has more caffeine per ml, but a full cup of drip coffee has more per serving. B hedges a little better ("often less"), cites both sources for the figures and names bean type as a factor. These are small differences, so they score about the same, with B slightly ahead.

The two answers are almost identical, and both give the right figures: espresso has more caffeine per ml, but a full cup of drip coffee usually has more in total. A says "often less", a hedge that fits better, since a double shot can match a cup of drip. A lists source [5] but never cites it. B never cites its listed source [4] and states the per-serving comparison as absolute. A is slightly better.

A gives the real fix: lubricate the hinge pin with oil, grease or WD-40. That advice is not in its sources, and it treats cabinet-hinge steps as if they applied to doors. B only repeats cabinet-installation steps it sourced and never mentions lubrication. Its conclusion that a squeak is fixed by reinstalling or adjusting hinges is wrong and not useful.

A never mentions lubrication, which is the usual fix. It mostly repeats cabinet-installation steps and pads with sources it admits are irrelevant. B gives the right fix: oil or grease the pivot and hinge pin. That advice isn't supported by its cited sources, and it slightly misstates source [1]. Still, B is far more useful.

Neither answer covers the "for good" part: preventing regrowth with ventilation, an extractor fan, humidity control or fixing leaks. Both give reasonable bleach-cleaning steps. B ties its claims to cited sources and adds detergent pre-cleaning and safe disposal, though its point about wood is a bit off-topic. A lists bare steps with no inline citations, so it is less grounded.

B's steps are clear and easy to read on a phone, and 1 cup per gallon is standard advice, but it has no inline citations. A is slightly better grounded.

A gives clear, correct steps, including dividing by a when a≠1, and a worked example that checks out. B leaves out the divide-by-a step but still adds (b/2)² for a general ax², which is wrong whenever a≠1. B's example is correct, but its single paragraph is harder to follow on a phone.

B is better. It gives correct, complete steps, including dividing by a when a≠1 and remembering the ± when taking the square root, and its worked example is right. A starts from ax²+bx+c but adds (b/2)² without dividing by a first, which gives the wrong result whenever a≠1. A also never mentions the ±.

Both give the date, the RBMK flaws and the botched test. Both repeat a doubtful "one million times radiation" claim, and neither mentions that Pripyat was evacuated the next day. A also explains thermal runaway and fallout across Europe, so it is slightly more complete. B adds nothing over A.

Both claim radiation rose "nearly one million times" in Europe and North America. That is an exaggeration drawn from a groundwater source, and it is a serious error. B is slightly better: it explains thermal runaway, which ties back to the earlier reactor answer, and notes Europe-wide contamination. Both get the date, the test, and the RBMK design flaws right.

Both answers give the correct average of 384,400 km and the right perigee/apogee range, and both are well cited. A is slightly more precise because it names the semi-major axis and labels the perigee and apogee. B's line "consistently given" adds nothing. The difference is small, but A is a little better.

Both correctly give 384,400 km and the roughly 356,400–406,700 km range, with matching citations. B adds two accurate details: the average is the semi-major axis, and the extremes are perigee and apogee. A's "consistently given" adds nothing. The difference is small, so B is only slightly better.

Both answers correctly give 7.5 hours (600 ÷ 80) and show the same calculation. Both cite a road-trip tips source that probably doesn't support the arithmetic, which is a minor groundedness problem. The only difference is an uncited source in the list: A lists a metric/imperial page, B lists an irrelevant Fiat 600 page. That doesn't change the content, so it's a tie.

Both answers correctly give 7.5 hours (600 ÷ 80) and explain the formula clearly. Both also cite a road-trip tips page that probably doesn't support the number, but the arithmetic needs no source. They differ only in an unused fifth source: A lists Fiat 600, B lists metric/imperial equivalents. That difference doesn't matter, so it's a tie.

A gives accurate guideline steps: a rate of 100–120 per minute, 30:2 breaths, and keep going until help arrives. It leaves out hands-only CPR and the AED. B gives the rate as just 100 per minute, which is imprecise. It also omits the 30:2 ratio and when to stop, though it does mention hands-only CPR. A is more complete and easier to act on.

B gives the correct 100–120/min rate, the 30:2 compression-to-breath ratio, how to give breaths, and when to stop, in clear steps that are easy to read on a phone. A states a flat 100/min, which is slightly inaccurate, and leaves out the breath ratio and when to stop. A cites sources inline, but B is still more accurate and complete.

Both give the correct core steps: remove the heat source, cool for about 15 minutes, no grease or ointments, and cover with sterile gauze. B also says to put raw onion on the burn. That is an unproven folk remedy that could cause infection, and its only source is a home-remedies page. A is accurate and concise. Neither mentions when to seek medical care.

A suggests putting raw onion on the burn and says it prevents marks. That is an unproven folk remedy, cited only to an ethnomedicine source, and could cause harm or infection. B gives standard, safe steps, adds flushing with cool water, and makes no dubious claims. B is clearly better.

Both answers rightly say they have no live price. B is more useful because it points the reader to live trackers. However, it calls the January 2021 price "the latest" when its sources likely cover later dates. It also wrongly suggests those exchanges have traded Bitcoin since 2009. A is accurate but gives the reader nowhere to go next.

Both answers correctly say they have no live price. A is more useful: it tells the user to check a live tracker or exchange. But it overstates the January 2021 figure as the sources' "latest" price and implies exchange trading began in 2009. B is accurate but bare and offers no next step.

Both answers rightly say the sources don't mention Dr. Anna Keller's practice and don't invent a number. A also names the closest match, the Landhaus Keller restaurant, which explains the near-miss. Both wrongly say Trump was president in 2016; it was Obama, and both contradict themselves by noting Trump took office in January 2017. A mentions that the election was to replace Obama, which hints at the right answer. However, its vote shares (48.5%/46.4%) are slightly off from the usual 48.2%/46.1%. Neither answer is usable.

Both answers get the main fact wrong. Barack Obama was president in 2016; Trump took office in January 2017, which both answers admit, so they contradict themselves. B mentions Obama being replaced, which gives the reader a hint. However, B's vote shares (48.5% vs 46.4%) differ slightly from the reported figures (48.2% vs 46.1%). Both fail the question.

B is better. It gives clearer, more practical steps: get out of the water, rinse with vinegar, don't use fresh water, scrape off the stingers with gloves, and get help if the sting is serious. A covers the vinegar rinse but adds a vague line about the tropics and leaves out the other steps. Neither answer mentions soaking in hot water or which symptoms mean emergency care.

A gives more practical steps: get out of the water, rinse with vinegar, avoid fresh water, scrape off stingers safely and get help if symptoms continue. B is thinner and includes a vague 'preserve life' line that doesn't tell the reader what to do. Neither mentions hot-water soaking for pain or which symptoms are emergency signs.

B gives the right main fix: lubricate the pivot and tighten loose screws. Its sealant/foam advice and the gate-hinge note are irrelevant and stretch the sources. A takes the whole hinge off instead of just pulling and greasing the pin. That is needless work, and A's steps don't clearly match its cited sources. B gives a coherent fix: clean the pin, lubricate it, refit the hinge. Removing the whole hinge is overkill, since tapping out the pin is enough. A's core advice (lubricate, tighten screws) is right, but it adds misleading sealant/foam advice and irrelevant teardrop-trailer hinge material, and cites kitchen-cabinet sources for a door question.
